claims.claim: When future L2/3 neurons are induced to localize in L5, they do not acquire the characteristics of L5 neurons.
claims.source: Another relevant observation is that when future L2/3 neurons were induced to localize in L5, they did not acquire the characteristics of L5 neurons (Ramos et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claims.claim: A substantial amount of TCAs grow into the Relnrl/Relnrl mutant CP, although they pass a bizarre course.
claims.source: In this mutant, a substantial amount of TCAs was reported to grow into the mutant CP, although they pass a bizarre course (Caviness and Frost, 1983), which could be enough to induce L4 specification.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claims.claim: L4 specification may occur in postmitotic neurons.
claims.source: Although it has long been supposed that cell fate decision of cortical neurons takes place mainly in the progenitor cells (Dehay and Kennedy, 2007; Molyneaux et al., 2007), our data now suggest that L4 specification may also occur in postmitotic neurons
claims.evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence including postmitotic Pcdh20 expression and function.

claims.claim: The distribution of Pcdh20-knockdown neurons remains normal before and during radial neuronal migration but becomes disrupted after neurons settle beneath the MZ.
claims.source: Consistent with this finding, the distribution of the Pcdh20-knockdown neurons remained normal before and during radial neuronal migration, but became disrupted after the neurons settled beneath the MZ.
claims.evidence: Supported by time-course experimental data.

claims.claim: Introduction of the Pcdh20-knockdown vector even in a postmitotic population causes misspecification of L4 neurons.
claims.source: Moreover, introduction of the Pcdh20-knockdown vector even in a postmitotic population caused misspecification of the L4 neurons.
claims.evidence: Supported by BrdU labeling experiment data.

claims.claim: Expression of Pcdh20 in postmitotic neurons is able to rescue the phenotypes induced by Pcdh20 knockdown.
claims.source: Finally, expression of Pcdh20 in the postmitotic neurons was able to rescue the phenotypes induced by Pcdh20 knockdown.
claims.evidence: Supported by Tα1 promoter rescue experiment data.

claims.claim: Many subtype-specific genes play roles in postmitotic neurons.
claims.source: This idea, of postmitotic regulation of subtype specification, is also supported by the fact that many subtype-specific genes play roles in postmitotic neurons (Alcamo et al., 2008; Arlotta et al., 2005; Britanova et al., 2008; Kwan et al., 2008; Lai et al., 2008; Leone et al., 2014)
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: There is a high level of plasticity in the identity of postmitotic cortical neurons.
claims.source: and that there is a high level of plasticity in the identity of postmitotic cortical neurons (De la Rossa et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claims.claim: Future L4 neurons have the capacity to differentiate into L2/3 neurons even in the postmitotic stage.
claims.source: These observations suggest that "future L4 neurons" have the capacity to differentiate into L2/3 neurons even in the postmitotic stage.
claims.evidence: Inferred from Pcdh20-knockdown neurons acquiring L2/3 characteristics.

claims.claim: Laminar fates are regulated, at least in part, in the progenitor cells.
claims.source: Our results, however, also suggest regulation, at least in part, of the laminar fates in the progenitor cells, because the Pcdh20-knockdown "future L4 neurons" had "imperfect" characteristics as compared to the normal L2/3 neurons, such as poorly developed basal dendrites and relatively mild conversion of the axonal projection patterns in the knockdown neurons located in L2/3.
claims.evidence: Inferred from incomplete conversion of L4 to L2/3 characteristics.

claims.claim: The effect of dominant-negative RhoA mimics the failure in neuronal positioning induced by Pcdh20 knockdown.
claims.source: We observed that the effect of dominant-negative RhoA mimicked the failure in neuronal positioning induced by Pcdh20 knockdown
claims.evidence: Supported by DN-RhoA experiment data.

claims.claim: CA-RhoA is able to restore the phenotypes of Pcdh20-knockdown neurons.
claims.source: and that CA-RhoA was able to restore the phenotypes of the Pcdh20-knockdown neurons.
claims.evidence: Supported by CA-RhoA rescue experiment data.

claims.claim: The relationship between protocadherin and RhoA has been shown in other systems.
claims.source: The relationship between protocadherin and RhoA has also been shown in other systems (Chung et al., 2007; Unterseher et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Loss of Pcdh20 primarily leads to dysregulation of dendritic morphogenesis, followed by malpositioning of L4 neurons.
claims.source: We assume that the loss of Pcdh20 primarily leads to dysregulation of dendritic morphogenesis, followed by malpositioning of the L4 neurons
claims.evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence including in vitro morphology changes.

claims.claim: Pcdh20 knockdown in an in vitro culture results in increased dendritogenesis without altering L4 fate specification.
claims.source: First, Pcdh20 knockdown in an in vitro culture, where cell positional effects are ignorable, resulted in increased dendritogenesis without altering L4 fate specification.
claims.evidence: Supported by in vitro culture experiment data.

claims.claim: Pcdh20- and Dcx double-knockdown neurons tend to exhibit pyramidal morphology even if they are in L4, especially those located near the margin of L4.
claims.source: In vivo, Pcdh20- and Dcx double-knockdown neurons tended to exhibit pyramidal morphology even if they were in L4, especially those located near the margin of L4, also suggesting the primary effect, to some extent at least, of Pcdh20 on cell morphology.

claims.claim: Regulation of dendritic morphogenesis by another protocadherin was reported previously.
claims.source: Regulation of dendritic morphogenesis by another protocadherin was also reported previously (Shima et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claims.claim: Loss of Pcdh20 first affects dendrite morphology leading to extensive dendritic arborization when control cells start to exhibit simplification of their complex apical primitive dendrites.
claims.source: Second, in the time-course experiment of Pcdh20 knockdown, we noticed that loss of Pcdh20 first affected the dendrite morphology leading to extensive dendritic arborization, when the control cells already started to exhibit simplification of their complex apical primitive dendrites (Figure 2J,K).
claims.evidence: Supported by time-course experiment observations shown in Figure 2J,K.

claims.claim: Active RhoA rescues the malpositioning caused by Pcdh20 knockdown with reduced arborization of the apical dendrites.

claims.evidence: Supported by CA-RhoA rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The abnormal dendrites might have caused the Pcdh20-knockdown neurons to become 'stuck' to the MZ.
claims.source: Because the arborized dendrites were predominantly found in the MZ, it is possible that the abnormal dendrites might have caused the knockdown neurons to become 'stuck' to the MZ.
claims.evidence: Speculative reasoning based on dendrite localization.

claims.claim: Several members of the protocadherin family exhibit homophilic binding activity.
claims.source: Considering that several members of the protocadherin family exhibit homophilic binding activity (Kim et al., 2007; Morishita and Yagi, 2007; Suzuki, 2000; Takeichi, 2007)
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Homophilic interactions may regulate laminar formation through gathering neurons that share the adhesion activity.
claims.source: it is conceivable that homophilic interactions may regulate laminar formation through gathering neurons that share the adhesion activity.
claims.evidence: Speculative reasoning based on known protocadherin properties.

claims.claim: The interactions through protocadherins, including Pcdh20, are usually very weak or undetectable.
claims.source: However, since the interactions through protocadherins, including Pcdh20, are usually very weak or undetectable (K.O. and K.N. unpublished data), there may be other ligands that activate Pcdh20 to regulate neuronal positioning.
claims.evidence: Supported by unpublished data from the authors.

claims.claim: There may be other ligands that activate Pcdh20 to regulate neuronal positioning.
claims.source: However, since the interactions through protocadherins, including Pcdh20, are usually very weak or undetectable (K.O. and K.N. unpublished data), there may be other ligands that activate Pcdh20 to regulate neuronal positioning.

claims.claim: The acquisition of L4-specific characteristics by future L4 neurons coincides with the arrival of TCAs into the lower part of the CP.
claims.source: Since the acquisition of the L4-specific characteristics (e.g., simplification of apical dendrites) by the "future L4 neurons" coincided with the arrival of the TCAs into the lower part of the CP (Lopez-Bendito and Molnar, 2003), we hypothesized that these axons could positively regulate the L4 identity specification.

claims.claim: TCAs are involved in correct subtype specification of L4 neurons.
claims.source: We demonstrated here that TCAs might be involved in correct subtype specification of L4 neurons by the analysis of TCA-deficient Pcdh10 (OL-pc) knockout mice.

claims.claim: TCAs instruct the development of modality-specific properties of cortical neurons.
claims.source: and that TCAs instruct the development of modality-specific properties of cortical neurons (Pouchelon et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claims.evidence: Supported by analysis of Pcdh10 (OL-pc) knockout mice.

claims.claim: A transmembrane protein is involved in subtype specification in the post-migratory stage.
claims.source: Finally, another intriguing finding of this study was the apparent involvement of a transmembrane protein in the subtype specification in the post-migratory stage.

claims.claim: The environment around immature neurons could influence the subtype specification of neurons.

results.result: Pcdh20 is preferentially expressed in layer 4 (L4) of the neocortex postnatally and shows weak expression during early embryonic development, with strong expression beginning only at late stages of radial migration toward the marginal zone.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 are supported by converging evidence from in situ hybridization (Figure 1A-D) and quantitative RT-PCR (Figure 1E) showing temporal and spatial expression patterns. The data consistently demonstrate low embryonic and high postnatal expression in L4, with appropriate controls including sense probes.

results.result: PC20sh effectively knocks down Pcdh20 expression in both overexpression systems and primary cortical cultures, while a mutant control (PC20sh_mut) does not affect Pcdh20 levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C8 are supported by multiple complementary approaches including immunoblotting (Figure 2A,C) and RT-qPCR (Figure 2B) demonstrating specific knockdown. The inclusion of mutant control (PC20sh_mut) strengthens specificity claims.

results.result: Pcdh20 is required for correct positioning of future L4 neurons in a cell-autonomous manner, as demonstrated by knockdown causing malpositioning to superficial layers and rescue by RNAi-resistant Pcdh20.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C15 are supported by in vivo electroporation experiments (Figure 2D-G) with multiple controls including mutant shRNA, alternative targeting sequences, rescue experiments, and layer-specific analysis. The cell-autonomous nature is demonstrated by sequential electroporation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).

results.result: Ectopic expression of Pcdh20 in L2/3 neurons does not reposition them to L4 but causes broader distribution within L2/3, indicating Pcdh20 alone is insufficient for L4 positioning.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C18 are supported by ectopic expression experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F). This negative result is important for understanding Pcdh20 function and suggests additional factors are required, though the mechanism remains unclear.

results.result: Pcdh20 functions primarily in the post-migratory stage, as knockdown effects on neuronal positioning are not evident during migration (E16.5-E18.0) but become apparent after neurons settle beneath the marginal zone (P2).
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C21 are supported by time-course experiments (Figure 2H-M) showing normal positioning during migration but malpositioning post-migration. This temporal analysis is critical for understanding when Pcdh20 acts, though the exact molecular events remain to be determined.

results.result: Pcdh20-knockdown neurons lose L4 molecular markers (Rorb, KCNH5) while maintaining normal thalamocortical axon growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C26 are supported by immunohistochemistry at P7 (Figure 3A-E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The loss of L4 markers is quantified and statistically significant. However, the claim about TCA growth (C25) is based on qualitative assessment without quantification.

results.result: Pcdh20-knockdown neurons acquire L2/3 molecular characteristics, including increased expression of Lhx2, Satb2, and Tbr1.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C30 are supported by immunohistochemistry showing increased L2/3 markers (Figure 3F-N, Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The quantification shows statistically significant increases. This represents a key finding demonstrating fate conversion at the molecular level.

results.result: Laminar marker expression differences between control and Pcdh20-knockdown neurons become evident by P2 for Rorb but not for Lhx2, indicating temporal progression of specification.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C34 are supported by developmental time-course immunohistochemistry (Figure 3—figure supplement 1M-T). The data show that specification is not complete at E18.0 but begins by P2, supporting the post-migratory specification model.

results.result: Pcdh20 knockdown causes future L4 neurons to acquire L2/3 axonal projection patterns, with increased contralateral projections demonstrated by retrograde tracing.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C39 are supported by Fluoro-Gold retrograde tracing experiments (Figure 4A-D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1). The data show statistically significant increases in contralateral projections. This functional assay complements molecular marker data, though the incomplete conversion noted elsewhere suggests partial fate change.

results.result: Pcdh20-knockdown neurons exhibit pyramidal morphology and electrophysiological properties resembling L2/3 neurons rather than the stellate morphology of L4 neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C44 are supported by biocytin labeling (Figure 4E-G, Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and electrophysiology (Figure 4H). Multiple parameters show L2/3-like characteristics. Sample sizes are adequate (n=9-16 cells), though biological replicates are not clearly stated.

results.result: Pcdh20 knockdown causes incomplete conversion of L4 to L2/3 characteristics, as evidenced by small cell size (membrane capacitance) and poorly developed basal dendrites compared to normal L2/3 neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C47 are supported by electrophysiology (Figure 4H) and morphology (Figure 4F,G). The incomplete conversion is an important finding suggesting partial specification in progenitors, though alternative explanations (e.g., timing of knockdown) are not fully excluded.

results.result: Pcdh20 knockdown perturbs L4 specification in postmitotic cells without affecting cell cycle progression, as demonstrated by BrdU pulse-chase experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C51 are supported by BrdU labeling experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-D). The experimental design appropriately identifies postmitotic cells, and the lack of effect on BrdU-negative cell proportions rules out cell cycle effects. This is critical evidence for postmitotic function.

results.result: Postmitotic expression of Pcdh20 using a neuron-specific Tα1 promoter is sufficient to rescue malpositioning phenotypes, demonstrating that postmitotic Pcdh20 function is essential.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C53 are supported by rescue experiments using Tα1 promoter (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E,F). This is strong evidence for postmitotic function, though the timing of Tα1 promoter activation and potential perdurance of earlier expression are not fully addressed.

results.result: RhoA signaling is required for correct L4 positioning, as dominant-negative RhoA mimics Pcdh20 knockdown phenotypes, suggesting they function in the same pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C56 are supported by DN-RhoA experiments (Figure 5A,B). The similar phenotypes suggest pathway involvement, though this is correlative. The claim of same pathway (C56) is inferential and requires additional epistasis experiments for definitive proof.

results.result: DN-RhoA does not affect neuronal positioning at E18.0, indicating its effects occur post-migration, similar to Pcdh20.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C58 are supported by time-course analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). However, the authors acknowledge concentration/condition dependencies and note a non-significant trend toward deeper positioning, suggesting potential migration effects that complicate interpretation.

results.result: Constitutively active RhoA rescues both malpositioning and loss of Rorb expression caused by Pcdh20 knockdown, indicating RhoA functions downstream of Pcdh20.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C61 are supported by CA-RhoA rescue experiments (Figure 5C-H). The rescue of both positioning and molecular markers is strong evidence for downstream function. However, the epistasis is not complete proof of direct pathway relationship, as parallel pathways could converge.

results.result: Dcx knockdown causes random neuronal positioning and demonstrates that ultimate cell position determines L4 vs L2/3 characteristics, with 72% of neurons in L4 expressing Rorb regardless of Dcx knockdown.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C67 are supported by Dcx knockdown experiments (Figure 6A-N, Figure 6—figure supplement 1). The position-dependent marker expression (C66) is particularly strong evidence. However, Tbr1 not changing (C64-C65) suggests some markers may have position-independent regulation.

results.result: Neurons accidentally positioned in L4 by Dcx knockdown express Rorb even without Pcdh20, demonstrating that Pcdh20 controls L4 specification indirectly through positioning.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C69 are supported by double knockdown experiments (Figure 6O-Q, Figure 6—figure supplement 1N-P). This is a critical experiment demonstrating indirect specification through positioning. The logic is sound, though the incomplete rescue suggests additional complexity.

results.result: Pcdh20 knockdown does not affect Rorb expression in vitro, indicating Pcdh20 requires in vivo cellular environment to specify L4 identity through controlling cell positioning.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C72 are supported by in vitro culture experiments (Figure 6R). The lack of effect in vitro is strong evidence for position-dependent specification. However, the culture conditions may not fully recapitulate in vivo environment, and the timing of culture initiation (E18.0) may miss earlier specification events.

results.result: Pcdh20-knockdown neurons have increased neurite numbers in vitro culture, suggesting Pcdh20 may directly regulate neuronal morphology to some extent.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C74 are supported by in vitro morphology analysis (Figure 6S-U). This suggests a direct morphological effect independent of positioning. However, the claim of 'direct' regulation (C74) is inferential, as the in vitro system may not exclude all positional cues.

results.result: Thalamocortical axons (TCAs) provide positional cues for L4 specification, as demonstrated by loss of L4 markers and acquisition of L2/3 markers in TCA-deficient Pcdh10 knockout mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C81 are supported by analysis of Pcdh10 (OL-pc) knockout mice (Figure 7A-K). The correlation between TCA loss and L4 specification failure is strong. However, the causal claim (C76, C81) is inferential based on correlation and temporal coincidence (C75), not direct manipulation of TCAs.

results.result: The authors propose a model where L2/3 and L4 identities are specified post-migration according to cell position, with future L4 neurons positioned via Pcdh20-RhoA signaling and specified by TCA signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C86 represent the authors' integrative model (Figure 7L). The model is well-supported by the collective experimental evidence, though some elements remain speculative (particularly TCA signaling mechanism, C85). The model represents a significant conceptual advance but requires further validation.

results.result: Previous studies show that Reeler mutant cortex contains normal neuronal subtypes despite disorganized lamination, and that TCAs grow into Reeler cortex, which may explain L4 specification in this mutant.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C89 are supported by citations to previous literature. These claims provide important context for interpreting the current results and address potential contradictions. However, the authors' interpretation of why Reeler has L4 neurons (C89) is speculative.

results.result: L4 specification occurs in postmitotic neurons, as evidenced by postmitotic Pcdh20 expression, post-migration timing of effects, postmitotic knockdown causing misspecification, and postmitotic rescue, though some progenitor-level regulation also occurs.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C97 synthesize multiple lines of evidence for postmitotic specification. The evidence is strong and converging (C91-C93 supported by data, C94-C95 by citations). The acknowledgment of incomplete conversion (C97) and progenitor contribution is appropriately cautious.

results.result: RhoA functions in the Pcdh20 pathway, as demonstrated by DN-RhoA mimicking Pcdh20 knockdown and CA-RhoA rescuing Pcdh20 knockdown phenotypes, consistent with protocadherin-RhoA relationships in other systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C99 are supported by experimental data (Figures 5A-H), and C100 by citations. This represents a mechanistic advance, though the molecular details of Pcdh20-RhoA interaction remain unclear. The epistasis experiments are well-designed.

results.result: Pcdh20 loss primarily affects dendritic morphogenesis, leading to excessive arborization and malpositioning, as evidenced by in vitro dendritogenesis, time-course morphology changes, and CA-RhoA rescue with reduced arborization.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C106 are supported by multiple lines of evidence (in vitro culture, time-course, rescue experiments). The mechanistic model is well-reasoned. However, C107 (neurons 'stuck' to MZ) is speculative. The primary vs. secondary nature of morphology effects remains somewhat uncertain.

results.result: Protocadherins exhibit homophilic binding that may regulate laminar formation, though Pcdh20 interactions are weak or undetectable, suggesting other ligands may activate Pcdh20.
results.evaluation: Claim C108 is supported by citations, but C109 and C111 are speculative. C110 is supported by unpublished data, which cannot be evaluated. The speculation about alternative ligands (C111) is reasonable but unsupported. This represents an important gap in understanding Pcdh20 activation.

results.result: TCAs are involved in L4 specification based on temporal correlation of TCA arrival with L4 maturation and phenotypes in TCA-deficient mice, consistent with previous studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C116 are supported by temporal correlation (C112, with citation), Pcdh10 KO analysis (C113, C116), and citations (C114-C115). The evidence is strong but largely correlative. The mechanism of TCA action remains unclear, and the role of synaptic activity is debated.

results.result: Previous studies suggest synaptic activity from TCAs is not required for L4 specification in mice, though complete blockade perturbs later development while initial specification appears normal.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C118 are supported by citations to previous literature. These claims provide important context for interpreting TCA function, suggesting non-synaptic mechanisms may be involved. However, the authors note timing differences between cited studies and their observations.

results.result: A transmembrane protein (Pcdh20) is involved in post-migratory subtype specification, suggesting environmental influence on neuronal identity, though whether transcription factors are induced intrinsically or environmentally remains unknown.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C120 are supported by the collective experimental evidence showing Pcdh20 (a transmembrane protein) functions post-migration. C121 identifies an important knowledge gap. This represents a conceptual advance in understanding environmental contributions to cell fate.
